Facial Aesthetics

Microneedling: Benefits, Process, and Aftercare

Learn what professional microneedling is designed to treat, what the procedure feels like, and which safety and recovery details matter.

August 25, 20263 min readPublished by The House of Dental

Microneedling reaches below simple exfoliation

Professional microneedling uses many fine needles to create controlled punctures in the skin. The repair response can increase collagen production and improve the appearance of selected acne scars, wrinkles, and uneven texture. Devices that penetrate living skin are different from short, blunt rollers marketed only for surface exfoliation.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has cleared specific microneedling devices for particular uses and age groups. Clearance does not apply to every device, body area, or product combination. It also does not mean the treatment is appropriate for everyone.

What happens during an appointment

A consultation comes first. The provider reviews the skin concern, medical conditions, medications, history of cold sores or unusual scarring, and the products currently used at home. Active infection, certain immune or bleeding problems, uncontrolled diabetes, and some skin conditions may make treatment unsuitable or require added precautions.

A topical numbing medicine is often applied before the procedure. The device is passed over the treatment area at settings chosen for the skin and the treatment goal. A new sterile cartridge should be used for each session. The procedure may feel scratchy or warm, and pinpoint bleeding can occur.

Professional microneedling should not be treated as a casual do-it-yourself service. Devices that reach deeper tissue can contact blood vessels and nerves. Training, infection control, device authorization, and a plan for complications are part of safe treatment.

Early recovery is visible

Redness or darkening of the treated skin, mild swelling, tightness, dryness, and a sunburn-like sensation are common after treatment. These effects often settle over several days, although recovery varies with needle depth and individual skin response.

The skin barrier is temporarily more reactive. Follow the provider's instructions for cleansing, moisturizer, sunscreen, makeup, exercise, and active ingredients such as retinoids or acids. Applying an unapproved product to freshly treated skin can increase irritation and may change how deeply ingredients penetrate.

Results and risks need equal attention

Improvement develops gradually as the skin remodels, and a series of treatments may be recommended. Results vary, maintenance may be needed, and no responsible plan can promise that a scar or wrinkle will disappear.

Less common problems include infection, persistent pigment changes, scarring, a cold sore flare, or an unwanted cosmetic result. Seek medical guidance for increasing pain, drainage, blisters, spreading redness, fever, or a reaction that is getting worse rather than settling.

Radiofrequency microneedling uses needles to deliver heat and has a different risk profile. The FDA issued a 2025 safety communication after reports of serious complications with certain uses. Anyone considering that treatment should ask exactly which device and technology will be used.

How it differs from nearby options

A chemical peel uses a solution to remove selected skin layers. Laser resurfacing uses light energy and can treat tissue at different depths. Microneedling relies on mechanical punctures and does not target pigment with heat in the same way, although post-treatment pigment changes can still occur.

The best comparison starts with the type and depth of the concern, skin tone, tolerance for downtime, history of scarring, and the evidence for the proposed device. Choosing a procedure by trend or by a dramatic social media result leaves out most of the information that affects safety.

Sources and further reading

  1. U.S. Food and Drug Administration: Microneedling Devices
  2. American Academy of Dermatology: Microneedling
  3. FDA: Potential Risks with Certain Uses of RF Microneedling
